nodes.content: Infer spatial conductivity and unknown boundary flux from sparse temperature observations while preserving uncertainty under nonidentifiability.
requirements: Achieve 90% interval coverage within five percentage points for conductivity and flux across identifiability regimes.
Match known-flux conductivity reconstruction error within 20% when joint recovery is identifiable.

nodes.content: Use joint Bayesian heat-equation inversion with log-Gaussian-process conductivity, spline flux, and ridge-aware MCMC to retain conductivity–flux tradeoff uncertainty.
Do 12 interior thermistors across two forcing schedules separate conductivity modes from unknown flux splines without overconfident intervals?
Two forcing schedules with 12 thermistors yield 85–95% marginal coverage across regimes and ≤1.2× known-flux conductivity RMSE when identifiable.
Simulate 12-thermistor HeatID under two schedules and three regimes; benchmark joint conductivity–flux 90% coverage and conductivity RMSE against known-flux inversion.
Run 200 HeatID replicates across three regimes and both schedules; score ridge-aware MCMC conductivity/flux coverage and known-flux-relative conductivity RMSE.
Across 200 two-schedule HeatID replicates, weak-regime flux 90%-interval coverage was 72%; identifiable conductivity RMSE was 1.14× known-flux.
A hierarchical flux-spline roughness prior should lift weak-regime flux coverage from 72% to 85–95% while retaining ≤1.2× known-flux conductivity RMSE.
Refit 200 two-schedule HeatID replicates using hierarchical flux-spline roughness; benchmark regime-specific conductivity/flux coverage and known-flux-relative conductivity RMSE.
Refit 200 HeatID replicates with hierarchical roughness and baseline priors; compare regime-specific 90% coverage and known-flux-relative conductivity RMSE.
After longer chains, baseline achieved 87–93% conductivity/flux coverage across regimes and 1.16× known-flux RMSE; hierarchical weak-flux coverage stayed 79%.
Does hierarchical roughness over-shrink weak-regime flux uncertainty, or is its 79% coverage caused by persistent ridge-mixing failure?
Contrast weak-flux coverage (initial 72%, extended-baseline 87–93%, hierarchical 79%) using matched-chain prior swaps, ridge ESS, and interval widths.
Using n13's three-benchmark contrast, run 200 matched-chain HeatID prior swaps; measure conductivity/flux coverage, ridge ESS, interval widths, and identifiable RMSE.
Broad-hyperprior hierarchical refits attained 88% weak-flux coverage (previously 79%), ridge ESS 520, and 1.17× known-flux conductivity RMSE.
Treat initial 72% coverage as chain-length sensitivity and hierarchical 79% as prior over-shrinkage; adopt broad-hyperprior refits achieving 88%.
Optimize thermistor placement and controlled boundary-temperature schedules using joint Fisher-information eigenvalues, retaining posterior uncertainty along unresolved conductivity–flux modes.
Can optimized placement and boundary-temperature schedules resolve conductivity–flux ridges with 12 thermistors without sacrificing weak-regime interval coverage?
Fisher-optimized 12-thermistor layouts and schedules increase minimum joint-information eigenvalue twofold while preserving 85–95% coverage and ≤1.2× RMSE.
Fisher-optimize 12-thermistor layouts and forcing schedules; assess minimum eigenvalue, 90% coverage, and known-flux-relative RMSE across 200 HeatID replicates.
Optimized HeatID designs raised the minimum joint-information eigenvalue 2.3×; conductivity/flux coverage was 87–94%, with identifiable conductivity RMSE 1.12× known-flux.
Are Fisher-optimized layouts robust to 2-mm thermistor misplacement and temporally correlated noise, or does weak-regime flux coverage deteriorate?
Stress-test optimized HeatID designs with 2-mm sensor offsets and AR(1) noise (ρ=0.6), measuring 90% coverage and known-flux-relative RMSE.
Run 200 optimized-design HeatID replicates with ±2-mm sensor offsets and AR(1) noise (ρ=0.6); assess regimewise 90% coverage and known-flux-relative RMSE.
Under 2-mm offsets and AR(1) noise (ρ=0.6), optimized designs yielded 78% weak-flux coverage and 1.26× known-flux conductivity RMSE.
Retain optimized designs for calibrated settings (87–94% coverage); 78% weak-flux coverage and 1.26× RMSE under perturbations require redesign.
Robust Fisher designs modeling sensor offsets and AR(1) noise should restore 85–95% conductivity/flux coverage and ≤1.2× known-flux conductivity RMSE.
Which nuisance drives weak-flux undercoverage in optimized designs: ±2-mm thermistor misplacement or AR(1) noise (ρ=0.6)?
Before redesign, compare calibrated and perturbed HeatID benchmarks in 2×2 ablations of ±2-mm offsets and AR(1) noise (ρ=0.6).
Run 200 HeatID replicates per ±2-mm-offset × AR(1)-noise cell, comparing nominal versus robust-Fisher designs on flux coverage and conductivity RMSE.
Nominal calibrated weak-flux coverage was 90%; AR(1)-only yielded 80%, offsets-only 88%; robust joint design achieved 83% and 1.24× known-flux-relative RMSE.
Quantify AR(1) and offset main effects and interactions on weak-flux coverage, then refit noise-only HeatID cases with AR(1) likelihoods.
Estimate main and interaction effects; refit 200 AR(1)-only robust-design HeatID replicates with AR(1) likelihood; score flux coverage and conductivity RMSE.
AR(1) reduced weak-flux coverage by 10 points versus offsets’ 2; AR(1)-aware refits reached 89% coverage and 1.18× known-flux RMSE.
Prioritize AR(1)-aware likelihood over sensor repositioning: noise costs 10 coverage points versus offsets’ 2; validate combined perturbations separately.
Train a conditional diffusion posterior on 12-thermistor heat-equation simulations, marginalizing AR(1) noise and sensor offsets while representing conductivity–flux ridges.
Can diffusion posteriors marginalizing AR(1) noise and sensor offsets achieve 85–95% weak-flux coverage without erasing conductivity–flux ridges?
Nuisance-marginalized diffusion will achieve 85–95% weak-flux coverage, preserve ridge correlation within 0.1 of MCMC, and ≤1.2× known-flux RMSE.
Train diffusion on 50,000 HeatID simulations spanning three regimes, AR(1) ρ∈[0,0.7], and ±2-mm offsets; benchmark against calibrated MCMC.
Train HeatID diffusion on 50,000 nuisance-randomized simulations; evaluate 200 held-out cases for weak-flux coverage, ridge correlation, and known-flux-relative RMSE.
On 200 held-out HeatID cases, diffusion gave 81% weak-flux coverage, ridge-correlation error 0.18, and 1.15× known-flux conductivity RMSE.
Add ridge-aligned score weighting and held-out quantile calibration; re-evaluate weak-flux coverage, ridge-correlation error, and known-flux-relative RMSE.
Retrain HeatID diffusion with ridge-weighted scores; calibrate quantiles on separate cases, then score 200 held-out cases against n38 thresholds.
Ridge-weighted, calibrated diffusion attained 89% weak-flux coverage, 0.08 ridge-correlation error versus MCMC, and 1.16× known-flux conductivity RMSE.
Does pooled 89% weak-flux coverage hide undercoverage when AR(1) correlation reaches 0.7 alongside 2-mm sensor offsets?
At ρ=0.7 with 2-mm offsets, pooled-calibrated diffusion will yield below 85% weak-flux coverage despite its pooled 89%.
Compare original 81% and calibrated 89% diffusion coverage using stratified HeatID tests at ρ=0.7 and ±2-mm offsets.
Run 200 weak-regime HeatID cases (ρ=0.7, ±2-mm offsets); compare original and calibrated diffusion coverage, ridge-correlation error, and conductivity RMSE.
At ρ=0.7 and ±2-mm offsets, calibrated diffusion yielded 82% weak-flux coverage versus 89% pooled; ridge-correlation error was 0.11.
Defer pooled diffusion deployment: calibration raised coverage from 81% to 89%, but stressed cases reached only 82%; require nuisance-stratified calibration.
Use PDE-constrained penalized profile likelihood with AR(1) noise and sensor offsets, bootstrapping conductivity–flux confidence bands along nonidentifiable ridges.
Can bootstrapped profile bands retain 85–95% coverage under weak identifiability and AR(1) noise without exceeding 1.2× known-flux conductivity RMSE?
Block-bootstrapped profile bands will attain 85–95% conductivity/flux coverage across HeatID regimes and ≤1.2× known-flux conductivity RMSE when identifiable.
Fit PDE-constrained conductivity/flux profiles with AR(1) likelihoods; block-bootstrap 200 HeatID replicates per regime and compare known-flux RMSE.
Fit AR(1)-aware PDE profiles and block-bootstrap 200 HeatID cases per regime; compute 90% conductivity/flux coverage and known-flux-relative RMSE.
HeatID-ProfileBench v1 contains block-bootstrap conductivity/flux bands, regime-specific 90% coverage, ridge profiles, and known-flux-relative conductivity RMSE.
Audit HeatID-ProfileBench v1 against truth for 85–95% regimewise conductivity/flux coverage, ridge-band widths, and ≤1.2× known-flux conductivity RMSE.
ProfileBench v1 yielded 92% weak-flux coverage but 81% weak-conductivity coverage; identifiable conductivity RMSE was 1.13× known-flux.
Use ridge-adaptive bootstrap critical values to address 81% weak-conductivity coverage; reassess flux coverage and identifiable known-flux-relative RMSE.
Recalibrate ProfileBench v1 ridge-specific bootstrap critical values on 200 HeatID cases per regime; reassess conductivity/flux coverage and identifiable RMSE.
Ridge-calibrated ProfileBench achieved 88–94% conductivity/flux coverage across regimes, including 89% weak-conductivity, and 1.13× known-flux identifiable RMSE.
Do ridge-calibrated profile bands retain 85–95% coverage when true boundary flux has sharp pulses absent from the fitted spline basis?
Despite weak-conductivity coverage rising from 81% to 89%, unmodeled 10-minute flux pulses will lower weak-flux coverage below 85%.
Simulate 10-minute boundary-flux pulses outside ProfileBench's spline basis; compare ridge-calibrated 90% bands across regimes against smooth-flux controls.
Using ProfileBench v1, fit ridge-calibrated bands to 200 pulsed and 200 smooth HeatID cases per regime; score conductivity/flux coverage.
Pulsed HeatID retained 87% weak-flux coverage (smooth: 92%); conductivity/flux coverage spanned 87–94%, with identifiable RMSE 1.15× known-flux.
Adopt ridge-calibrated ProfileBench: weak-conductivity coverage rose 81%→89%, pulsed weak-flux coverage remained 87%, and identifiable RMSE was 1.15× known-flux.
Combine AR(1)-whitened ensemble Kalman inversion with sensitivity-nullspace inflation and identifiability-stratified conformal bands for conductivity and flux.
Can nullspace-inflated Kalman ensembles achieve 85–95% conductivity/flux coverage under weak identifiability without breaching 1.2× known-flux RMSE?
Nullspace-inflated, stratified-conformal Kalman inversion yields 85–95% regimewise conductivity/flux coverage and ≤1.2× known-flux conductivity RMSE.
Implement AR(1)-whitened Kalman updates, inflate low-singular-value conductivity–flux modes, then conformal-calibrate bands within HeatID identifiability strata.
Fit 256-member AR(1)-whitened Kalman ensembles; calibrate strata on 300 HeatID cases and test 200 per regime for coverage and RMSE.
HeatID yielded 84% weak-conductivity and 91% weak-flux coverage; identifiable conductivity RMSE was 1.10× known-flux.
Recalibrate weak-conductivity bands using singular-mode-specific conformal scores on independent HeatID cases; verify coverage reaches 85–95% without increasing identifiable RMSE.
Calibrate singular-mode conductivity scores on 300 fresh HeatID cases; retest 200 per regime for 90% coverage and known-flux-relative RMSE.
Singular-mode calibration raised weak-conductivity coverage from 84% to 89%; regimewise conductivity/flux coverage was 87–93%, identifiable RMSE 1.10× known-flux.
Does identifiability-stratified calibration remain valid when sensor offsets shift a case into the wrong conductivity–flux singular-value stratum?
Compare pre/post singular-mode calibration under ±2-mm sensor offsets, tabulating stratum transitions, conductivity/flux coverage, and identifiable RMSE.
Inject ±2-mm offsets into 200 HeatID cases per regime; measure singular-stratum reassignment, 90% coverage, and known-flux-relative conductivity RMSE.
Offsets reassigned 12% of cases; weak-conductivity/flux coverage remained 87%/89%, and identifiable RMSE was 1.16× known-flux.
Adopt singular-mode calibration: it corrected 84% weak-conductivity coverage to 89%; ±2-mm offsets retained 87–89% coverage and 1.16× RMSE.
